Guilty by Condition? Mental Illness, Criminal Responsibility and the Insanity Defence under Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS

~Divyansh Milind Vyas



This article examines how Indian criminal law treats accused persons with mental illness through the insanity defence under Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code and its successor, Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. It argues that these provisions remain rooted in the nineteenth century M’Naghten model and construct a narrow category of “legal insanity” that excludes many serious psychiatric conditions. Combined with the presumption of sanity in the Evidence Act and a heavy evidentiary burden on the accused, this framework means that mental illness often becomes a liability rather than a shield. Cases from the Superior Courts, along with empirical studies of insanity pleas and prison data, shows that successful reliance on the defence is rare and closely tied to prior access to diagnosis, treatment records and expert testimony.

Moving beyond doctrinal analysis, the article situates these rules within carceral realities and a developing rights framework under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Comparative glimpses from Canada and the United Kingdom illustrate alternative models that integrate mental disorder into procedure, sentencing and post-verdict supervision. The article proposes a shift from a binary insanity exception to a continuum of responsibility, with early screening, structured psychiatric evidence, specialised forensic services, sentencing guidance and disability sensitive training. It concludes that no one should be “guilty by condition” simply because the legal system fails to recognise and accommodate mental illness.





I. Introduction: From Narrative Injustice to Doctrinal Puzzle

Imagine waking up behind bars with only fragments of memory. The voices from the night before still echo in your head. You are told that you stabbed a neighbour. You remember fear and confusion. You do not remember intent. The criminal process now reads your life through the language of guilt, not of illness. The charge sheet records your act. It does not record your symptoms.

In Indian trial courts, scenes like this are not rare. The courtroom is supposed to be a space where guilt and innocence are decided on evidence and principle. Yet when the accused lives with a serious mental condition, the trial often becomes a test of credibility and normality. Lawyers whisper that the accused is “putting it on”. Judges watch posture and eye contact. Families carry old prescriptions to court and hope that someone will see them as more than paper. You captured this experience earlier with the phrase “guilty by condition”. The illness that should invite protection instead becomes one more reason to distrust the accused.

During an internship in a Delhi trial court, I watched a criminal defence lawyer represent a man with a long history of schizophrenia. The man had attacked a neighbour during a psychotic episode. When I asked whether the court would consider his condition, my senior replied that the law allows it but the people in the courtroom often do not. The family struggled to prove what they had struggled for years to manage. Police records described the man as dangerous. Medical records were incomplete. The defence of insanity existed on paper. It did not exist in practice for that accused.

This article situates that lived experience within the legal structure of Indian criminal law. The central provisions are old Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 and its successor Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023. Both provisions state that nothing is an offence if, at the time of doing the act, the person, “by reason of unsoundness of mind,” is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law. Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act 1872 places the burden of proving the exception on the accused. These rules promise protection for those who are genuinely unable to understand their actions. In reality, they make relief dependent on a very narrow conception of insanity and on evidence that many accused cannot produce.

The research questions are therefore simple but unsettling. First, does the insanity defence under Indian law meaningfully protect persons with mental illness. Second, has the replacement of “unsoundness of mind” in the Indian Penal Code with Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita changed anything of substance. Third, how do evidentiary rules and criminal process convert mental illness into a legal burden rather than a shield.

The argument of this article is that Indian law still treats mental illness in a rigid and under inclusive way. Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS remain rooted in the nineteenth century M’Naghten model of criminal insanity. This model focuses on a narrow idea of cognitive understanding. It neglects volitional impairment, fluctuating symptoms and many forms of psychiatric disability. When this narrow test is combined with the evidentiary burden under Section 105 and with weak mental health infrastructure, the result is that many accused with serious mental illness are more likely to be convicted, not less. They are, in effect, “guilty by condition”.

This introduction sets out the structure that follows. Part II explains the doctrinal framework of Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS and links them to the M’Naghten tradition and to the Mental Healthcare Act 2017. Part III traces how the Supreme Court and High Courts have interpreted the insanity defence and the burden of proof in leading cases such as Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v State of Gujarat and Bapu v State of Rajasthan. Part IV examines how procedure, proof and stigma convert mental illness into a legal handicap across arrest, trial and sentencing. Part V turns to prisons and shows how carceral institutions now function as de facto psychiatric facilities with little capacity for care. Part VI offers brief comparative glimpses from Canada and the United Kingdom. Part VII draws on the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and disability rights instruments to propose a more rights consistent model of criminal responsibility. Part VIII concludes by returning to the opening vignette and asks what it would mean for Indian criminal law to treat mental illness as a reason for support rather than as an aggravating condition.



II. Doctrinal Framework: Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS

A. Colonial origins and the M’Naghten template

Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 is the starting point of the insanity defence in Indian law. The provision was drafted in colonial India under the influence of the English M’Naghten rules of 1843. These rules presumed that an accused person is sane unless he can show that, at the time of the act, his mental condition was such that he did not know what he was doing or did not know that it was wrong. Section 84 IPC adopts the same structure. It excuses the accused only if, at the time of the act, “by reason of unsoundness of mind,” he or she was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law.

Over time, Indian courts have interpreted “unsoundness of mind” as a legal term. It has no formal definition in the Penal Code. In practice, courts treat it as equivalent to insanity in a narrow sense. The Supreme Court in Hari Singh Gond v State of M.P stressed that not every mental disorder counts. The Court drew a distinction between legal insanity and medical insanity. Only the former can attract Section 84. This approach reflects the M’Naghten legacy. Psychiatry may describe a wide range of conditions. The law accepts only a small subset as relevant to criminal responsibility.

The influence of Section 84 has extended far beyond India. A comparative study shows that Pakistan and Bangladesh have retained almost identical text.The continuity highlights the colonial origins of the provision and underscores how slowly doctrines of criminal insanity have evolved in the subcontinent. Indian criminal law developed long before modern psychiatry. The doctrinal history confirms that the insanity defence has remained closely tied to nineteenth century ideas about mind and responsibility.



B. The structure and elements of Section 84 IPC

Section 84 IPC contains several distinct elements. First, there must be an “act” that would otherwise amount to an offence. Second, at the time of doing that act, the accused must suffer from “unsoundness of mind.” Third, this condition must render the accused incapable of knowing either the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law.

The temporal requirement is strict. The focus is on the mental state at the exact time of the act. Later or earlier episodes of illness are relevant only as evidence. They are not sufficient by themselves. In Bhikari v State of Uttar Pradesh and later decisions, the Supreme Court and High Courts have repeatedly stressed that the crucial point of time is the moment of the offence, judged through conduct before, during and immediately after the incident.

Courts also begin with a presumption of sanity. This presumption is not spelled out in Section 84 itself. It flows from general principles and from Section 105 of the Evidence Act. Section 105 states that when an accused relies on an exception, such as unsoundness of mind, the burden is on the accused to prove facts that bring the case within the exception. Illustration (a) to Section 105 gives a direct example. It describes an accused who pleads that, by reason of unsoundness of mind, he did not know the nature of the act. The illustration clarifies that the burden is on the accused.

In Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v State of Gujarat, the Supreme Court harmonised Section 84 and Section 105. The Court held that the prosecution always bears the general burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. At the same time, the accused bears a special burden to prove insanity on a balance of probabilities in order to claim the benefit of Section 84. The accused can discharge this burden through oral, documentary or circumstantial evidence. If that evidence raises a reasonable doubt about the existence of the necessary mens rea, the accused is entitled to acquittal.

In practice, however, the interaction of Section 84 and Section 105 creates a high evidentiary hurdle. Accused persons with serious mental illness often come from poor and marginalised backgrounds. They may never have had access to psychiatric diagnosis or regular treatment. Medical records are scarce. Families may have avoided hospitals due to stigma. Courts see no past records and conclude there was no illness. The legal test remains formally neutral. Its application is structurally biased against those least able to prove their condition.



C. Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: new code, old language

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaces the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024. Section 22 of the new code is titled “Act of a person of unsound mind.” It states that nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law. The wording is, in substance, identical to Section 84 IPC. There is no express reference to “mental illness” in the text of Section 22, despite public discussions that often describe it in those terms.

At first glance, one might expect the new code to align more closely with the Mental Healthcare Act 2017. That Act defines mental illness in detailed and contemporary terms. It includes substantial disorders of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impair judgment, behaviour or capacity to meet ordinary demands of life. It also requires that determinations of mental illness follow nationally or internationally accepted medical standards, such as the World Health Organization’s ICD classifications.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita does not adopt this definition. Instead, it carries forward the older phrase “unsoundness of mind” from Section 84. The disjunction between the criminal code and the mental health statute is significant. It signals that criminal responsibility remains governed by a separate and narrower vocabulary. Mental health law embraces diagnostic complexity and a rights-based approach. Criminal law retains a binary category that is tied to the M’Naghten model and to a strict cognitive standard.



D. Setting up the critique

The continuity between Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS is striking. On paper, India has enacted a new criminal code. In relation to insanity, however, the law has changed very little. The same language of “unsoundness of mind” survives. The same focus on knowledge of the nature and wrongfulness of the act remains. The same evidentiary structure under Section 105 of the Evidence Act still applies, now read with a new code rather than with the IPC.

This article therefore treats Section 22 BNS not as a fresh start but as a restatement of an old doctrine in a new statute. The critical question is not only what the text says but how courts interpret and apply it. The next Part turns to that case law. It shows that the Supreme Court and High Courts have built a jurisprudence that is cautious, sometimes sympathetic, but overall restrictive. Mental illness is recognised in principle. In practice, many accused remain “guilty by condition” because the test is hard to satisfy and the evidence is hard to produce.



III. Judicial Construction of Legal Insanity in India

A. Burden of proof and the presumption of sanity

Indian courts approach insanity pleas through a dual burden structure. The prosecution must always prove the ingredients of the offence beyond reasonable doubt. At the same time, the accused who invokes Section 84 IPC or Section 22 BNS must prove facts that bring the case within that exception. This special burden flows from Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act 1872.

The Supreme Court explained this structure with clarity in Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v State of Gujarat. The Court held that there is no conflict between the general burden on the prosecution and the special burden on the accused. It laid down three propositions. First, the prosecution must prove the commission of the offence with the requisite mens rea beyond reasonable doubt. Second, there is a rebuttable presumption that the accused was sane at the time of the act. Third, the accused may rebut this presumption by placing oral, documentary or circumstantial evidence before the court. The standard for the accused is only that of a party in civil proceedings. If such evidence raises a reasonable doubt about any ingredient of the offence, the accused is entitled to an acquittal.

Section 84 and Section 105 therefore work together. The law presumes sanity and full responsibility. The accused must show that the case falls within the narrow category of legal insanity. This already shapes the insanity defence as an exception that must be actively proved. It is not a background principle. The presumption of sanity is strong in both doctrine and practice. Courts often repeat that every person is presumed to know the natural consequences of their acts and to know the law.



B. Legal insanity, not medical insanity

The Supreme Court has repeatedly stressed the distinction between legal insanity and medical insanity. In Hari Singh Gond v State of Madhya Pradesh, the Court held that “unsoundness of mind” in Section 84 IPC is treated as equivalent to insanity, but that the term itself has no precise medical definition. Not every person with a mental disorder is exempt from criminal responsibility. The court is concerned with legal insanity, not with medical insanity.

This position was reaffirmed in Surendra Mishra v State of Jharkhand. The Court stated that an accused who seeks the protection of Section 84 must prove legal insanity. The judgment explains that many conditions, such as odd or irritable behaviour, episodic fits, or a weak intellect, are not enough. There must be an inability to know the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law at the relevant time.

High Courts continue to rely on this distinction. Recent decisions echo Surendra Mishra and emphasise that abnormal conduct or a vague history of mental problems does not suffice. Courts look for clear evidence that meets the strict legal test. This approach reflects a consistent doctrinal line. It also narrows the class of cases in which mental illness can excuse criminal responsibility.



C. Narrowing the defence: rejection in borderline cases

Several Supreme Court decisions demonstrate how tightly courts apply Section 84. In Bapu @ Gajraj Singh v State of Rajasthan, the accused was described by witnesses as suffering from unsoundness of mind. The Court accepted that some evidence pointed to mental problems. It nevertheless held that the crucial question was the accused’s capacity at the time of the offence. It found no reliable proof that he was then incapable of understanding the nature of his act. The insanity defence was rejected.

In Surendra Mishra, the defence produced medical prescriptions and letters from a psychiatric institute. The trial court and High Court concluded that there was no clear finding on the degree and nature of the alleged illness. The Supreme Court agreed. It held that without specific, credible medical evidence the plea of insanity could not be accepted.

Hari Singh Gond shows the same pattern. Witnesses spoke of the accused’s unusual behaviour. The Court acknowledged that ‘insanity’ is a broad term, but insisted that the defence must show incapacity with respect to the nature and wrongfulness of the act. Mere odd or violent conduct was not enough. Since there was no convincing proof of such incapacity at the time of the killing, the Court upheld the conviction.

These cases do not deny the existence of mental illness. They simply refuse to treat it as sufficient for legal insanity. The result is a jurisprudence in which many mentally ill accused fall between categories. They are not ‘insane’ in the narrow legal sense. At the same time, their conditions clearly affect their perception and control. Many such people are “guilty by condition” because their illness draws suspicion rather than protection.



D. When the defence succeeds: schizophrenia and structured evidence

There are also cases where the Supreme Court has extended the benefit of Section 84. These tend to involve severe and well documented illnesses such as schizophrenia. In Shrikant Anandrao Bhosale v State of Maharashtra, the Court accepted evidence that the accused, a police constable, had long suffered from paranoid schizophrenia. Government doctors deposed on the basis of medical records that his condition existed before and after the offence. The Court held that the defence had established a reasonable doubt about his capacity at the time of the act and acquitted him.

In State of Rajasthan v Shera Ram @ Vishnu Dutta, the accused had a history of mental illness, including treatment and records from earlier years. His brother and doctors testified to episodes of ‘fits of insanity’. The Supreme Court emphasised that conduct before, during and after the offence, along with medical evidence, can support an inference of insanity at the critical time. The Court concluded that the prosecution had withheld relevant material and that the defence had met the standard of preponderance of probabilities. It gave the benefit of Section 84 and ordered directions for treatment under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

More recent decisions, such as Devidas Loka Rathod v State of Maharashtra and Rupesh Manger (Thapa) v State of Sikkim, reiterate that the accused need not prove insanity beyond reasonable doubt. A reasonable doubt about legal sanity is enough. These judgments also criticize investigative failures where obvious signs of mental illness are not followed up by timely psychiatric examinations.

The pattern is clear. Courts are more receptive to insanity pleas when they see a combination of factors. These include a long and documented history of severe illness, formal psychiatric diagnosis, treatment records, and witness accounts of bizarre conduct close to the time of the offence. Accused persons who cannot produce such a record rarely succeed.



E. Trial courts, appellate courts and structural disadvantage

Empirical work confirms this restrictive picture. A study of High Court judgments between 2007 and 2017 found that out of 102 cases where the insanity defence was raised, High Courts accepted the plea in only 18 cases. The success rate was about 17.65 per cent. In 76 cases, the insanity plea failed and the conviction stood. The study also showed that three factors were associated with success. These were a favourable lower court verdict, documentary evidence of mental illness before the crime, and a psychiatrist’s expert opinion.

Later analyses and commentaries have reached similar conclusions. They note that insanity pleas are rare, are often raised in serious offences such as murder, and succeed only when the record is unusually strong. Contrary to public perception, the defence is not a simple loophole. It is a narrow route that is difficult to navigate.

From the perspective of accused persons with mental illness, this case law has two important effects. First, it keeps the doctrinal bar high. The accused must show legal insanity in a strict sense, not merely medical impairment. Second, it ties success to access to diagnosis and treatment before the crime. Those with stable families, resources and proximity to mental health services are more likely to have the necessary records. Those who have been poor, homeless or socially isolated are less likely to do so. The formal rules appear neutral. Their effect is not. Mental illness becomes a liability in the courtroom because it is difficult to prove in the form the law demands.



IV. Process, Proof and the “Legal Burden” of Mental Illness

A. Mental illness as evidentiary handicap

The doctrinal framework would be demanding even in a well-resourced system. In the Indian criminal process, it operates within conditions of delay, overcrowding and limited legal aid. For an accused with mental illness, this combination turns the formal burden into a heavy practical handicap.

An accused person has to narrate their history to counsel, to doctors and sometimes to the court. Many cannot give a coherent account. Symptoms such as thought disorder, hallucinations, paranoid fear or severe depression affect memory, concentration and trust. Families may have partial stories and scattered prescriptions. Police officers may focus on confession and recovery of weapons, not on health. The investigative file that reaches the court often contains little systematic information on the accused’s mental condition.

The law, however, expects the defence to produce proof of legal insanity. In cases like Surendra Mishra and Hari Singh Gond, courts stressed the absence of reliable medical evidence and of clear findings on the nature and degree of illness. The result is a cycle. Because the system does not invest in early psychiatric evaluation, there is no robust evidence. Because there is no robust evidence, the defence fails.



B. Myths of the “fake insanity defence” and empirical reality

Popular media often portray the insanity defence as a trick. Films and news reports suggest that accused persons pretend to be mentally ill in order to escape punishment. Some academic writing also frames Section 84 IPC as a loophole that ‘cunning criminals’ exploit.

The empirical evidence does not support that image. The High Court study noted above found a success rate of about 17 per cent. Most insanity pleas failed. Another analysis of national trends between 2018 and 2020 suggested a national success rate of around 17 per cent and highlighted regional differences that correlated with mental health infrastructure. States with better psychiatric services saw slightly higher rates of successful pleas.

Commentaries in Indian psychiatry and criminal law journals echo these findings. They argue that the real risk in India is under use and under acceptance of insanity pleas, not over use. This matches the picture that emerges from case law. Insanity is accepted only when evidence is unusually clear. The fear of fabricated pleas often seems greater than the actual incidence of abuse.



C. Stages of criminal process where mental illness drops out

Mental illness can be relevant at many stages: arrest, bail, trial, sentencing and post-conviction supervision. Indian criminal process gives it a structured role at only two points. These are the determination of fitness to stand trial under Sections 328 to 339 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the substantive defence of insanity under Section 84 IPC or Section 22 BNS. In practice, even these provisions are unevenly applied. At the stage of arrest and remand, police officers may note that the accused behaves oddly. They rarely treat this as a trigger for mandatory psychiatric assessment. Unless the behaviour is extreme, the accused is processed like any other suspect. There is no routine screening. Legal aid lawyers may lack the time or training to identify red flags. Bail decisions tend to focus on gravity of offence and risk of flight. Mental illness is often seen, if at all, as a reason to deny bail, not as a reason to divert the accused to treatment.

At trial, mental illness appears in one of two ways. It may arise through a fitness to stand trial inquiry. Or it may enter as part of a Section 84 plea. Both depend on someone raising the issue. Courts seldom initiate these inquiries on their own. Once the trial moves past the evidence stage, attention shifts to legal classification and sentencing.

Sentencing in India has very little structured consideration of mental illness outside the death penalty context. In cases like Accused X v State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court has recognised that executing a prisoner who has developed severe mental illness violates Article 21 of the Constitution. For ordinary terms of imprisonment, however, there is no detailed sentencing guideline that asks courts to consider diagnosis, treatment needs or risk of deterioration in prison.

After conviction, the accused enters a prison system in which mental health services are scarce. Official data from the National Crime Records Bureau show that about 1.6 to 1.7 per cent of prisoners were recorded as having mental illness in recent years. Independent reports and investigative journalism suggest that the true prevalence is much higher and that many posts for psychologists and psychiatrists remain vacant.

These gaps show that the legal system treats mental illness as a narrow doorway at the guilt stage. If the accused does not fit through that doorway, their condition is often ignored at later points. This is another sense in which they become “guilty by condition”. The illness does not vanish after conviction. It simply ceases to attract structured legal attention.



D. When illness becomes liability in practice

Mental illness can harm an accused person’s position in many subtle ways. Judges and lawyers may perceive a person with disorganized speech or unusual affect as evasive or dishonest. Police officers may interpret fear or withdrawal as lack of cooperation. Witnesses may exaggerate the dangerousness of the accused because of stigma. Some recent trial court and High Court decisions still describe mentally ill accused persons in language that frames them as unpredictable threats rather than as rights holders.

These perceptions affect the assessment of credibility. They also influence decisions on bail and sentencing. An accused with a serious diagnosis may be seen as more likely to re-offend. Courts may therefore incline toward custody rather than supervised release, even when the legal test for insanity is not met.

All of this interacts with the doctrinal structure described in Part III. The law presumes sanity. The accused must show legal insanity with clear evidence. At the same time, stigma and fear encourage courts and prosecutors to treat mental illness as a risk factor rather than a vulnerability. The person with mental illness carries a double burden. They must prove enough illness to meet the strict legal test. They must not seem so ill that they appear dangerous, manipulative or beyond help.

Seen in this light, “guilty by condition” is not only a metaphor. It describes a pattern in which the fact of mental illness increases the accused’s exposure to punishment. It makes it harder to raise a successful defence. It makes it easier to justify pre-trial detention and harsh sentencing. It makes it less likely that prisons will invest in treatment



V. Reality of Mental Illness Behind Bars

A. Scale of the problem

The Indian criminal process often ends in imprisonment. For people with mental illness, prison is not only a site of punishment. It becomes a substitute mental health institution. Official data show that this population is not small. The Prison Statistics India 2023 report of the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) records that 9,095 inmates, about 1.7 per cent of a total prison population of 5.30 lakh, were identified as having mental illness in 2023. Most of them were undertrials. The percentage has hovered between 1.4 and 1.7 per cent for several years.

Independent analysis suggests that these numbers understate the problem. A recent IndiaSpend investigation, relying on NCRB data and the Supreme Court’s Centre for Research and Planning, noted that 9,084 of 5.73 lakh prisoners in 2022, or about 1.6 per cent, were recorded as having mental illness. It also reported that the Centre for Research and Planning had estimated around 16,503 prisoners with mental illness by 2023. The same analysis showed that suicide accounted for about 80 per cent of unnatural deaths in prisons between 2017 and 2022

Human rights organizations and UN bodies have raised similar concerns. A 2024 commentary on India’s report to the UN Human Rights Committee noted that 9,084 prisoners, or 1.58 per cent of the prison population in 2022, were reported as mentally ill, most of them undertrials, and that these figures likely undercount the true prevalence because of flawed screening and reporting. A systematic review of non-communicable diseases in Indian prisons found a pooled prevalence of depression of nearly 49 per cent among prisoners in the studies reviewed. These numbers do not prove that all such prisoners meet any particular legal test of insanity. They do show that mental illness behind bars is widespread and that official figures capture only a fraction of it.



B. Conditions of confinement and the mental health gap

Conditions in many Indian prisons aggravate this vulnerability. Overcrowding, lack of privacy, poor sanitation and frequent violence are now well documented problems. A large proportion of inmates are undertrials who have not yet been convicted. NCRB data for 2023 indicate that about 74 per cent of prisoners were undertrials. These conditions are stressful even for healthy people. For those already struggling with psychosis, mood disorders or substance dependence, they can deepen distress and provoke crisis.



Mental health services in prisons have not kept pace with need. The IndiaSpend analysis found that two out of three sanctioned posts for psychologists and psychiatrists in prisons were vacant in 2022. Only nine women psychologists and psychiatrists were employed nationwide, most of them in a single state. The Model Prison Manual 2016, prepared by the Bureau of Police Research and Development, recommends one psychologist or counsellor for every 500 prisoners and mandates mental health screening on admission. Implementation has been uneven.

Recent public interest litigation in the Bombay High Court illustrates the gap between law and reality. In Dr Harish Shetty v State of Maharashtra, the Court examined compliance with the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 in relation to prisoners. It noted that only a few central prisons in the state had psychiatric wards and that only a handful of psychologist and psychiatrist posts had been sanctioned. The Court referred to advisories emphasising mental health literacy training for prison staff, protocols for identifying prisoners at risk of suicide and the need for regular reporting to Mental Health Review Boards. It also underlined that these frameworks remained largely on paper.

The result is a system in which mental illness is often discovered late, in conditions least suited to care. Prisons become the default holding spaces for people whose illnesses are not recognised early enough for diversion or treatment.



C. Constitutional and statutory obligations

Indian constitutional law does not treat prisons as law free zones. Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. The Supreme Court has long held that this includes a right to live with human dignity and to access basic health care, including mental health care, in state institutions.

The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 gives more specific content to these obligations. Section 18 recognises a right to access mental health care and treatment from health services run or funded by government. Section 103 deals directly with prisoners with mental illness. It requires that prisoners with mental illness be transferred to the psychiatric ward in the prison medical wing or to a mental health establishment for care and treatment. It also requires mental health establishments in prisons to be registered and to meet prescribed standards. The accompanying Rules of 2018 set minimum standards for prison mental health services. These include mandatory screening on entry, protocols for managing suicide risk and the availability of psychiatric medicines and psychosocial interventions.

Despite this legal framework, implementation remains partial. Commentators on forensic psychiatry in India note that Section 103 has not been fully operationalised and that many prisons lack registered mental health establishments or systematic reporting to Mental Health Review Boards. In effect, prisoners with mental illness occupy a legal space where rights are strong on paper and weak in practice.

The Supreme Court’s jurisprudence on the death penalty shows how mental illness can function as a partial check on the harshest punishments. In Accused X v State of Maharashtra, the Court commuted a death sentence where the prisoner had developed severe mental illness during years on death row. It held that executing such a prisoner would violate Article 21. Yet similar attention has not been systematically extended to the wider prison population living with mental illness.



D. From narrow defence to long term responsibility

When one places these carceral realities next to the doctrinal framework of Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS, a pattern emerges. Legal doctrine focuses on a single moment: the time of the act. If the accused cannot show legal insanity at that instant, they remain fully responsible and may be sentenced to long terms of imprisonment. Once inside, the law’s interest in their mental condition often recedes.

The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and related rules try to correct this by imposing duties on prison authorities. They require screening, treatment, transfer to mental health establishments and regular oversight. The gap between these norms and daily practice shows how difficult it is to move from a model centered on guilt to a model centered on long term responsibility and care.

This is another way in which mentally ill accused become “guilty by condition.” The law is incredulous at the stage where their illness could excuse or mitigate. It is inattentive at the stage where their illness needs sustained care.



VI. Comparative Glimpses and Normative Lessons

A. Canada: the NCRMD verdict and Review Boards

Canadian criminal law codifies the insanity defence in Section 16 of the Criminal Code. It states that no person is criminally responsible for an act or omission made while suffering from a mental disorder that rendered the person incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of the act or of knowing that it was wrong. The language is similar to Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS. It also presumes that every person does not suffer from a mental disorder that exempts them from responsibility, and it places the burden of proof on the party that raises the issue.

The key difference lies in what happens after the defence is established. Under Part XX.1 of the Canadian Criminal Code, if a court finds that an accused committed the act but was exempt from criminal responsibility by virtue of Section 16, it must render a verdict that the accused is “not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder” (NCRMD). This is neither a conviction nor a full acquittal. It is a third kind of verdict. The accused is then referred to a provincial or territorial Review Board, a specialized tribunal that includes a judge and at least one psychiatrist. The Board decides on dispositions such as hospital detention, conditional discharge or absolute discharge, and reviews these decisions at regular intervals.

The Supreme Court of Canada in Winko v British Columbia (Forensic Psychiatric Institute) described this system as one that recognises two principles. First, people who commit criminal acts under the influence of mental illnesses should not be held criminally responsible in the same way as sane offenders. Second, public safety may still require supervision or detention for some of them. The NCRMD regime tries to balance these aims through regular, individualized risk assessments.

For present purposes, two features are important. First, Canada treats mental disorder not only as a defence but also as a basis for a specialised post-verdict pathway. Second, responsibility for managing that pathway lies with tribunals that are structurally linked to mental health expertise rather than only to general criminal courts. Indian law lacks such an intermediate space. An accused who meets Section 84 or Section 22 is simply acquitted or dealt with through general provisions on detention of persons of unsound mind, with far less structured oversight.



B. United Kingdom: special verdict and disposal options

The United Kingdom retains the M’Naghten rules at common law. A person is legally insane if, at the time of the act, they were labouring under such a defect of reason, arising from a disease of the mind, that they did not know the nature and quality of the act or did not know that it was wrong. This test, like Section 84 IPC, is cognitive and narrow.

Procedure and disposal, however, are structured through statute. The Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 provides that where insanity is proved in the Crown Court, the jury must return a special verdict of “not guilty by reason of insanity.” The Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991 expands the court’s powers. Where a special verdict is returned or the accused is found unfit to plead but to have done the act, the court must order one of three disposals. These are a hospital order, with or without a restriction order, a supervision order, or an absolute discharge.

Hospital and restriction orders integrate criminal procedure with the Mental Health Act 1983. A hospital order with restrictions permits detention in a secure psychiatric facility with controlled discharge, subject to tribunal oversight. English criminal practice thus links the insanity verdict to a clear menu of health-oriented outcomes. Prosecutorial guidance from the Crown Prosecution Service also encourages attention to diversion and mental health at charging and sentencing stages, not only at the moment of the verdict.

Again, the substantive test of insanity remains narrow. Critiques in British scholarship argue that the M’Naghten rules are out of date, over inclusive for some neurological conditions and under inclusive for many serious mental illnesses. Reform discussions have proposed capacity-based tests and clearer links to human rights law. Yet the procedural framing already does something that Indian law does not. It gives courts structured tools to direct mentally disordered offenders toward hospitals, community supervision or discharge instead of leaving outcomes to ad hoc discretion.



C. Lessons and limits for Indian reform

Neither the Canadian nor the British model can be copied wholesale into the Indian context. Both operate in systems with far greater mental health infrastructure and different social support networks. They also face their own criticisms, including concerns about indefinite detention and the boundary between treatment and control.

For Indian law, the comparative value lies in three points. First, both systems acknowledge that mental disorder requires distinctive procedural treatment beyond a simple “guilty” or “not guilty” choice. Second, both link criminal responsibility doctrines to institutions that have mental health expertise, whether Review Boards in Canada or hospital order regimes in the United Kingdom. Third, they embed mental disorder in sentencing and supervision as well as in defences.

Current Indian law does some of this through the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and provisions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, but in a fragmented way. Sections 328 to 339 of the Code deal with unfitness to stand trial. Section 103 of the Mental Healthcare Act deals with prisoners with mental illness. Prison manuals speak of screening and counselling. What is missing is an integrated framework that treats mental illness as relevant along a continuum that runs from first police contact to final release, rather than as a narrow doorway of insanity under Section 84 or Section 22.

The comparative discussion therefore supports the central argument of this article. Indian law does not have to choose between complete exculpation and complete indifference. It can maintain a high standard for exculpation while still recognising mental illness as a reason for diversion, tailored sentencing and structured support.



VII. Reimagining “Guilty by Condition”, a Newer Model

A. Disability rights, mental health law and criminal justice

Indian criminal law does not exist in isolation. Since 2007, it operates within a broader disability rights framework. India signed the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) on 30 March 2007 and ratified it on 1 October 2007. The Convention requires States to promote, protect and ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disabilities. It includes people with long term mental, intellectual or sensory impairments whose interaction with barriers restricts participation in society.

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPwD Act) is Parliament’s main response. The Act gives effect to the UNCRPD in domestic law. It recognises disability as including mental illness. It affirms equality, non-discrimination, dignity and respect for integrity. The Supreme Court in Vikash Kumar v UPSC described the RPwD Act as a statutory manifestation of constitutional commitments under Articles 14, 19 and 21. The Court stressed that equality for persons with disabilities requires reasonable accommodation and positive support, not just formal non-discrimination.

The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (MHCA) carries the same rights-based logic into mental health law. It replaced the Mental Health Act 1987. It declares that every person has a right to access affordable, good quality mental health care without discrimination. It recognises legal capacity, informed consent, advance directives and supported decision making. Commentators describe the Act as a paradigm shift that aligns mental health law with the UNCRPD and moves away from a purely custodial model.

At the international level, Article 13 of the UNCRPD requires States to ensure effective access to justice for persons with disabilities. It calls for procedural and age appropriate accommodations at all stages, including during investigation and trial. It also calls for training of police, prison staff and others in the justice system. Scholarship on Article 13 emphasises that access to justice depends on recognition of equal legal capacity and participation, not on exclusion from the legal system.

Taken together, these instruments set a clear direction. Persons with mental illness are rights holders. They are entitled to support in exercising their rights. The State must remove barriers to their participation. Criminal courts and prisons are part of this obligation, not exceptions to it.



B. Misalignment between insanity doctrine and disability rights

The insanity defence in Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS does not sit easily with this rights-based framework. It is rooted in the older idea that some people lack reason altogether and must therefore be removed from the ordinary rules of responsibility. It uses the language of “unsoundness of mind” rather than the language of disability and support. The test is binary. Either the accused is so impaired that they cannot know the nature or wrongfulness of their act. Or they are treated as fully responsible, with mental illness playing little formal role.

The UNCRPD promotes universal recognition of legal capacity. It treats disability as a reason to provide support, not to withdraw recognition. Many legal systems still use status or functional capacity tests to deny legal agency to people with psychosocial disabilities. UN bodies have criticised such tests for embedding discriminatory assumptions about what counts as rational or acceptable decision making. Indian commentators on the RPwD Act have noted a tension within domestic law. On one hand, the Act presumes legal capacity and seeks to replace guardianship with supported decision making. On the other hand, various statutes still use “unsoundness of mind” as a ground for disqualification from office or for special treatment in criminal law. This mix produces a picture in which mental illness sometimes helps, sometimes hurts, and often confuses.

Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS illustrate this problem. They recognise that, in rare cases, mental illness can excuse crime. At the same time, they treat mental illness purely as incapacity. The test does not ask whether the accused could have acted differently with proper support, or whether their condition reduces culpability without removing it. It asks only whether the person was incapable of knowing the nature or wrongfulness of the act. If the answer is no, the illness may then reappear in sentencing as a reason to see the person as dangerous and in need of confinement.



C. From binary exception to continuum of responsibility

A rights consistent model would approach mental illness and criminal responsibility along a continuum. It would still recognise that some people at times lack the capacity needed for criminal responsibility. It would also recognise that many others have partial impairments that should affect how the system treats them, even if these do not amount to legal insanity.

The UNCRPD and Article 13 invite States to provide procedural accommodations and supports so that persons with disabilities can participate in justice processes. For mentally ill accused, this could mean early psychiatric assessment, clear communication, support persons in court, and adjustments to how evidence is taken. It could also mean that mental condition is recorded and considered at bail, at fitness to stand trial, at the guilt stage, at sentencing and in decisions about prison placement and release

The MHCA 2017 already gives some tools. It recognises advance directives and nominated representatives. It mandates the creation of State Mental Health Authorities and Mental Health Review Boards. It distinguishes between general hospitals and mental health establishments. These structures can support a continuum approach if criminal courts and prison administrations engage with them more closely. The problem is not only absence of law. It is also the weak integration of existing laws with criminal procedure and with evidence doctrines.



D. Concrete reforms within the Indian framework

Several reforms are conceptually modest yet could move practice much closer to the rights-based model described above. They build on existing statutes rather than replacing them.

First, early mental health screening should become routine at police stations and first appearance courts where there are indications of mental illness. The Code of Criminal Procedure already gives magistrates wide powers to order medical examination and to inquire into fitness to stand trial. Linking these powers with MHCA 2017 standards would ensure that people in acute distress are identified and diverted to treatment at an early stage.

Second, courts need clear, standardized tools to assess criminal responsibility and capacity. Practice directions from High Courts could require structured psychiatric reports that address the legal criteria under Section 84 and Section 22, rather than offering bare diagnostic labels. The Delhi High Court’s 2025 decision on a mentally disabled accused in a sexual assault case, which insisted on a proper inquiry under Section 330 CrPC, is an example of judicial insistence on procedure.

Third, states should designate and fund forensic mental health units and secure psychiatric wards in line with Section 103 of the MHCA 2017. This would reduce the use of ordinary prisons as holding spaces for severely ill accused and convicts. Recent High Court directions to implement the MHCA in full, including in Punjab and Maharashtra, show that courts are willing to push the executive on this point.

Fourth, sentencing guidelines should recognise mental illness as a mitigating factor and as a reason to prefer supervised treatment or community based orders in suitable cases. The Supreme Court’s reasoning in Accused X already accepts that mental illness can limit the moral legitimacy of the harshest punishment. Extending this reasoning beyond the death penalty would be consistent with both Article 21 and the RPwD Act.

Fifth, training is crucial. Article 13 of the UNCRPD calls for training for police, prison staff and justice actors. Judicial academies, police academies and prison training institutes can incorporate modules on mental illness, disability rights, and the correct use of Section 84 and Section 22. Recent Supreme Court and High Court judgments on disability and reasonable accommodation, including Vikash Kumar and subsequent cases, offer accessible material for such training.

Finally, legal aid systems must adapt. Many accused with serious mental illness rely on legal aid lawyers. These lawyers need both training and time to identify mental health issues, to collect medical evidence and to press for diversion or tailored sentencing where appropriate.

None of these reforms require abolition of the insanity defence. They require that the defence be embedded in a wider network of support and accommodation. In such a framework, mental illness would cease to function primarily as a reason to doubt the accused. It would become a reason for the system to adjust itself and to share responsibility for outcomes.



VIII. Conclusion

This article began with a simple image. A person wakes up in a cell, half remembering an act that may change their life. They are on trial not only for what they did, but for who they are. Their mental condition becomes part of the story that others tell about guilt and danger.

The analysis traced how Indian criminal law currently responds to such people. Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS adopt a narrow cognitive test of insanity. They focus on whether the accused, at the time of the act, was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. The Evidence Act presumes sanity and places the burden of proving insanity on the accused. Supreme Court case law reinforces this by insisting on strict proof of legal insanity and by distinguishing it sharply from medical diagnoses.

Empirical studies show that insanity pleas are rare and that most of them fail. Success is tied to prior access to diagnosis, to treatment records and to expert testimony. At the same time, prisons hold thousands of people with mental illness in overcrowded and under resourced conditions. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and the RPwD Act 2016 recognise these people as rights holders who are entitled to dignity, treatment and support. Implementation remains uneven.

Comparative models from Canada and the United Kingdom do not offer simple solutions. They do show that it is possible to treat mental disorder as more than a narrow defence. They integrate it into specialised procedures, post-verdict supervision and hospital-based dispositions. They link criminal responsibility to systems with mental health expertise. Indian law has the beginnings of such an approach in its mental health legislation and procedural codes. It has not yet woven these strands into a coherent whole.

The phrase “guilty by condition” captures the risk that mentally ill accused face in this landscape. Their condition makes it harder to meet the legal test for insanity, harder to instruct counsel, harder to produce records, and sometimes easier for the system to view them as dangerous. The reforms suggested in Part VII aim to invert that logic. They would treat mental illness as a trigger for support and procedural adjustment. They would place some responsibility back on the institutions that currently rely on prisons as default mental health providers.

The constitutional and international commitments are already in place. The challenge is to interpret and apply Section 84 IPC and Section 22 BNS in a way that is consistent with those commitments. A criminal justice system that takes disability rights seriously would still condemn deliberate wrongdoing. It would also accept that the State shares responsibility when it fails to recognise, support and accommodate mental illness before and after crime. No one should be more exposed to punishment simply because they are unwell.
